chapter: Los Angeles with Mutt Carey and the taxi dances
title: Why the saxophone drew him: Bix and Trumbauer
summary: Many clarinetists doubled on sax; Joe was fascinated by it and says Bix's records with Frank Trumbauer, heard in Los Angeles, set everybody off.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: Listening to you talk, you say that you got pretty early on the saxophone, and all that stuff. Did most of the clarinet players drop their clarinets when the saxophone became popular, or did some of them...?
No, a lot of them doubled. But it seems to me... I was fascinated with the saxophone then. I was just crazy about it. And really the guy that turned me on

to a saxophone (of course I had played it before) was when Bix Beiderbecke came out with "Singin' The Blues," with Frankie Trumbauer playing that C-melody. That's the record. "Singin' The Blues" was the name of it, and "Ida, Sweet As Apple Cider" -- that record just set everybody off.
Where did you hear that? Around here?

Right in Los Angeles. It wasn't made before... It was made in 1926, I believe. But when we heard that... I think he come out with two records, four sides, which was "Ida" and "Singin' The Blues" and two other tunes, I can't think of the name of them, but... Everybody wanted.... That was a distinctly new style. Bix really created a new style.
